abstract:
In lab-grown human neurons and organoids carrying CHD8 or SCN2A mutations, researchers reduced organoid overgrowth and moved neuronal electrical activity closer to wild-type levels.

The post Enhancer-Targeted CRISPR Turns Up Healthy Gene Copy in Autism Organoid Model appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Savannah Wiegel

content.value:
When a mutation hinders one copy of a gene, the remaining copy has to do the work of two. Researchers at UCLA have now shown, in lab-grown human brain cells, that a CRISPR-based tool could help that remaining copy in models of autism.

The proof-of-concept study, published in Nature Neuroscience, is titled “Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.” It was led by Daniel Geschwind, MD, PhD, at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. George Chen, PhD, now at Children’s Hospital of Los Angeles, is first author. Collaborators at the New York Genome Center and New York University also contributed.

“Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect,” the authors wrote. The team focused on two high-confidence autism genes: CHD8, which helps regulate other neurodevelopmental genes, and SCN2A, which is essential for neurons to fire electrical signals.

Instead of editing DNA, the researchers used CRISPR activation, pairing a catalytically inactive Cas9 with the activator p300 (dCas9-p300) to turn genes up without cutting them, and aimed it at fetal-brain enhancers. The team’s concern was that promoter targeting risks overexpression, a particular problem for haploinsufficient genes, which are often dosage sensitive.

“We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency,” the authors wrote. “Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology.”

In CHD8-mutant organoids, which grow abnormally large because progenitor cells overproliferate, treatment reduced organoid size in most treated lines and shifted gene expression toward wild-type patterns. In CHD8-mutant neurons grown in two-dimensional cultures, it increased markers of neuronal maturation. In SCN2A-mutant neurons, it showed restored excitability: firing approached wild-type levels in patient-derived neurons. Interestingly, “patient-derived iPSC neurons required higher current injections to achieve sustained firing compared to HUES66-derived neurons across conditions, indicating a line-dependent difference in baseline intrinsic excitability rather than incomplete functional rescue,” reported the authors.

“Our results show that, in human cell models, it’s possible to turn up that remaining copy and move cells back toward typical development,” Geschwind said in a press release. “This is a key first step, and it gives us a new way to think about addressing the biology underlying these conditions.”

The authors call the work “an important proof of principle” and note they were able to “moderately increase the expression of each gene.” However, “the effect of eCRISPR-A decreased over time,” and “an open question remains regarding the effect of introducing CRISPR-A after the expected peak in expression.” They say “further optimization of viral infection, constructs, and use of alternative Cas enzymes” would increase the approach’s clinical utility.

“We are still a long way from the clinic, and there is a lot of work ahead on delivery and timing,” added Chen in a press release, “but these findings provide hope and give us a clear direction.”
